title: The True Nature of All Phenomena
author: Zhanran
excerpt: The true nature of all phenomena is the fundamental principle of the Buddhadharma, and it is also the watershed that divides the Buddhadharma from the teachings of outsiders and of Mara. The Buddhist Numerical Dictionary says: "For the great Mahayana sutras spoken by the Tathagata all seal their teachings with the principle of true reality. Outsiders cannot adulterate them, heavenly maras cannot destroy them. If there is the seal of true reality, then it is the Buddha's teaching; if there is no seal of true reality, then it is Mara's teaching."

inline.s: The true nature of all phenomena is the fundamental principle of the Buddhadharma, and it is also the watershed that divides the Buddhadharma from the teachings of outsiders and of Mara. The Buddhist Numerical Dictionary says:

"For the great Mahayana sutras spoken by the Tathagata all seal their teachings with the principle of true reality. Outsiders cannot adulterate them, heavenly maras cannot destroy them. If there is the seal of true reality, then it is the Buddha's teaching; if there is no seal of true reality, then it is Mara's teaching."
Master Zhiyi's Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra says:

"As for the lesser-vehicle sutras, if they bear the seal of the three seals of impermanence, non-self, and nirvāṇa, then they are the Buddha's teaching, and one who cultivates them attains the Way; if they lack the three dharma seals, then they are Mara's teaching. A Mahayana sutra has only one dharma seal, namely the true nature of all phenomena; it is called a sutra of definitive meaning and can lead one to the great Way. If it lacks the seal of true reality, it is Mara's teaching."
(For a more detailed discussion of the true nature of all phenomena, see
Selected Annotations on the Sutra of the Treasury of the Buddha

Since ancient times, the philosophies of East and West alike have tirelessly sought the essence of the universe and all things. Yet Śākyamuni Buddha, more than two thousand years ago, already gave the correct answer:
The essence of the universe and all things is the true nature of all phenomena.
Looking at modern science, the Buddha's assertions are being confirmed one by one, which only makes the Buddha's great wisdom appear all the more ultimate and perfect.

blocks.text: 1. What Is the True Nature of All Phenomena

inline.s: The so-called "true reality" means the actual state of affairs; the "true nature of all phenomena" means the actual state of affairs of all phenomena. The Sutra of the Treasury of the Buddha says:
"What is called the true nature of all phenomena? It is that all phenomena are ultimately empty, without anything whatsoever."
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra says:
"All phenomena are like illusions; the Tathagata, amid them, by the power of skillful means, is stained by nothing."
The Lotus Sutra says:
"The great bodhisattvas contemplate all phenomena as empty, as true reality, neither inverted nor moving, neither retreating nor turning."

[Dharma] In Buddhist studies, "dharma" has several meanings: 1. It refers to things and phenomena, including both the material and the mental; 2. Law, principle, regularity; 3. The way of cultivation, that is, the principles, methods, and states of cultivating the Way; 4. It is synonymous with "the Way." 5. The mental objects among the six dusts (forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tactile objects, and mental objects). Which meaning is intended must be judged from the context. The "dharma" in "the true nature of all phenomena" refers to things and phenomena. [All phenomena] refers to the myriad things and phenomena, all that is arrayed before us.
[Emptiness] Having appearance but no substantial reality (like things in a dream) is called "emptiness." In the Sutra of Holding the World,
Chapter Three on the Eighteen Natures, the Buddha says:
"Knowing that all phenomena are empty, like illusions without reality, without any root."

When describing the existence of things, besides "existent" and "nonexistent" there is another case, namely illusion, such as things in a dream, which do not truly exist but have appearance without substantial reality; the concept of "emptiness" is used to describe this. Master Hanshan says:
"The Buddha spoke the word 'emptiness' to break people's attachment to things as truly existent, not to mean absolute nothingness or annihilation."
The Vimalakirti Sutra,
Chapter Three on the Disciples, says:
"All phenomena are ultimately without anything whatsoever; this is the meaning of emptiness."

In this passage, "all phenomena" means that appearances exist, and "ultimately without anything whatsoever" means that in reality there is nothing (ultimately, there is nothing at all). This state in which appearances exist but reality does not (illusion) is called emptiness. Master Hanshan gave a profound exposition of "emptiness is precisely illusion; illusion means that which exists but is not real," which is excerpted below:
"Your letter seeking instruction is most sincere. Yet you have not grasped the two words 'emptiness' and 'illusion' correctly
(accurately)

, and so you are not without obstruction regarding mind and objects, which is why your practice is hard to carry out. Now I will explain it clearly for you, and then you will understand with no further doubt. The so-called 'emptiness' is not the emptiness of absolute nothingness; it is just as the common saying goes, 'as if no one were beside him' — is it really true that no one is beside him? It is merely that
(simply)

he holds his head high and does not count that person in his eyes. The so-called 'illusion' is not the illusion of weird transformations; it means that which exists but is not real. It is like a peep-show box in the marketplace, out of which many figures are produced. Yet within that box there is originally nothing at all, and yet suddenly there they are; though they exist, they are not real. Since they are not real, they are fundamentally nonexistent, and because they are fundamentally nonexistent, we speak of emptiness. Hence it is said: 'Like an illusory man — it is not that there is no illusory man, but the illusory man is not a real man.' If a person is not real, is that not emptiness? The Buddha spoke the word 'emptiness' to break people's attachment to things as truly existent, not to mean absolute nothingness or annihilation. Fearing that people might fall into annihilationism, he further spoke the word 'illusion' to dispel that view of annihilation. Thus all phenomena of body and mind are empty because they are illusory, and because they are empty they are said to be like illusions."
(From the Collection of Dream Wanderings,
Instruction to Zhou Ziyin)

[Peep-show box] A wooden box containing rolled-up pictures, with a row of small round holes on top (three or four holes), each fitted with a magnifying lens. After customers pay, they all put their eyes close to the holes and look inside. The box owner then slowly turns the handle on the side of the box, and so one picture after another passes continuously before the viewer's eyes. Usually the pictures depict stories one after another.
From this we can know that emptiness and illusion are synonyms. The Heart Sutra says:

"When Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva was practicing the profound prajñāpāramitā, he illuminated the five aggregates and saw that they were all empty, and thus passed beyond all suffering and distress. Shariputra! Form is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from form; form is emptiness, emptiness is form. The same is true of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness."
The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra,
Chapter Eleven on the Study of Illusion, says:

"Subhuti, what do you think? Is form different from illusion? Are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness different from illusion? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One. ... Form is not different from illusion, illusion is not different from form; form is illusion, illusion is form. World-Honored One, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not different from illusion, and illusion is not different from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; consciousness is illusion, illusion is consciousness."
Comparing these two passages of scripture carefully, one knows that "emptiness" means precisely "illusion."

The true nature of all phenomena is the most ultimate truth, and so it is called the supreme meaning. Yet just as Copernicus declared in his day that the earth revolves around the sun rather than the sun around the earth, and people simply could not believe it — Bruno was even judged a heretic and burned to death for proclaiming this truth — so too the World-Honored One, in the Sutra of the Treasury of the Buddha,

Chapter One on the True Nature of All Phenomena, gave ten similes in succession to show how difficult it is for people to believe and understand the truth of the true nature of all phenomena. For example, one of the similes:
"Shariputra, suppose a person chews and swallows Mount Sumeru
(Mount Sumeru)

and can consume it entirely, and flies through space without harm — what do you think, is this rare? It is rare, World-Honored One! Shariputra, that all phenomena spoken by all Buddhas are unborn, unceasing, signless, and unconditioned, and that people believe and understand this, is far more rare."
Though it is hard to believe and understand, the true nature of all phenomena is the truth, the supreme and unsurpassable truth. In the Lotus Sutra, the Buddha says:
"The foremost, rarest, and most difficult to understand Dharma attained by the Buddha — only a Buddha together with a Buddha can fully fathom the true nature of all phenomena."

Therefore, if one tries to investigate and ponder the true nature of all phenomena with an ordinary person's wisdom, it is like a firefly burning Mount Sumeru: it can never set it alight. So the Buddha's disciples need only believe and accept the Buddha's words and practice according to the teaching!
Question: What is the nature of phenomena?

Answer: The nature of phenomena is the essential nature (essence) of all phenomena; it is another name for the true nature of all phenomena. The Sutra of the Kingly Dharma Spoken by the Buddha for King Prasenajit says:

"All phenomena are empty in essence, impermanent, and subject to destruction. Suppose a person in a night dream sees a lovely garden, mountains and rivers, crowds of people, dense forests and clear springs, halls and pavilions, all delightful; when he wakes
(wakes up)
he sees nothing at all."
The Great Jewel Heap Sutra,
Volume Sixty-Four, says:
"Neither coming nor going, nor arising — the Buddha can expound such a Dharma; though he says the essence of all phenomena is empty, the World Hero still causes them to cultivate the path."
The Moon Lamp Samādhi Sutra says:

"The essence of all phenomena is ever quiescent; ordinary people, lacking wisdom, cannot realize it. If one can settle the mind in quiescent concentration, that person always has the Buddha with him."
The Avatamsaka Sutra,
Chapter on Ascending Mount Sumeru, says:
"The nature of phenomena is originally empty and quiescent, neither grasped nor seen."
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
"Living beings and lands share one nature of phenomena."
The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says:
"The nature of phenomena is as previously explained: each phenomenon is empty, and they are all one emptiness; this is the nature of phenomena."
[World Hero] Another name for the Buddha.
Question: Since the nature of phenomena is empty, doing good and doing evil should make no difference. Why then should one still observe the five precepts and the ten wholesome deeds so diligently?

Answer: Ultimately speaking, doing good and doing evil make no difference, because both are matters within the dream of ignorance and are equally empty. But we are still within the dream of ignorance, and there doing good and doing evil differ greatly; we are governed by the law of cause and effect, good deeds bring good rewards and evil deeds bring evil rewards, and joy and sorrow are vividly clear, as if real. Our observance of precepts and cultivation is precisely for the sake of awakening, for removing delusion and inversion, and for waking from this delusive dream.
Question: What is the dharma realm?

Answer: As to the aspect of things, "dharma" means phenomena and "realm" means division: all things in the phenomenal realm each have their own distinct and different characteristics and cannot be confused with one another, which is called the "realm of phenomena." As to the aspect of principle, although phenomena are infinitely varied in appearance, they share one and the same nature, which is called the "realm of principle," that is, the true nature of all phenomena.
Question: What is the one true dharma realm?
Answer: The one true dharma realm is the term used by the Huayan school for the most ultimate principle, just as the Tiantai school speaks of the true nature of all phenomena.
Question: What is meant by dependent origination and emptiness of nature?

Answer: Dependent origination means that all phenomena arise from the convergence of many conditions; this is spoken from the aspect of things. Emptiness of nature means that all phenomena are inherently empty in nature and do not truly exist; this is spoken from the aspect of principle.

blocks.text: 2. The True Nature of All Phenomena Is the Fundamental Principle of the Buddhadharma

inline.s: The one great matter for which the Buddha appeared in the world was to guide all living beings to fully accomplish the Buddha Way. The Sutra of the Treasury of the Buddha says:
"The true nature of all phenomena, ultimately empty and quiescent, is precisely the Buddha Way."
The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom,
Volume Five, says:
"Apart from the true nature of all phenomena, all the remaining phenomena are called Mara."
The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom,
Volume Ten, says:
"The Buddhas of the three times all take the true nature of all phenomena as their teacher."
In the Lotus Sutra, the World-Honored One reveals: the three vehicles are skillful means, the one vehicle is real. The Lotus Sutra,
Chapter on Skillful Means, says:
"In the buddha lands of the ten directions, there is only the one vehicle Dharma; there is no second
(referring to the shravaka and pratyekabuddha vehicles)
and no third
(referring to the shravaka, pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattva vehicles)

, except as spoken by the Buddha as skillful means." "All Buddhas and Tathagatas, by the power of skillful means, within the one buddha vehicle distinguish and speak of three." "Only this one matter is real; the other two are not true."

The three vehicles are the lesser vehicle (that is, the shravaka vehicle), the middle vehicle (that is, the pratyekabuddha vehicle), and the great vehicle (that is, the bodhisattva vehicle). The one vehicle is also called the one buddha vehicle; it is the only teaching that can lead people to Buddhahood. The shravaka vehicle cultivates according to the Four Noble Truths and escapes birth and death; the pratyekabuddha vehicle cultivates according to the twelve links of dependent origination and escapes birth and death; the bodhisattva vehicle cultivates according to the six perfections and escapes birth and death; whereas the one buddha vehicle cultivates according to the true nature of all phenomena and perfectly accomplishes the Buddha Way.

In the Sutra of the Treasury of the Buddha, the World-Honored One gives very detailed instructions on what the true nature of all phenomena is, on how the true nature of all phenomena is the fundamental principle of the Buddhadharma, and on how to cultivate according to the true nature of all phenomena. Master Zhiyu's
Paraphrase of the Sutra of the Treasury of the Buddha
provides an excellent commentary on this sutra.

blocks.text: 3. The True Nature of All Phenomena Is the Supreme Meaning

inline.s: The true nature of all phenomena is the supreme meaning. The Buddha says:

"All phenomena are false; wherever they cease, that is called real, that is called true reality, that is called the dharma realm, that is called ultimate knowledge, that is called the supreme meaning, that is called supreme emptiness."
(The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra,
Volume Forty)
[Supreme meaning] The supreme, perfect, and ultimate truth.
The Buddha says:
"All phenomena are like illusions, like dreams, like echoes, like shadows, like mirages."
(The Perfection of Wisdom Sutra in a Small Compass,
Volume Ten,
Chapter Twenty-Seven on Sadaprarudita)
The Buddha says:
"Knowing that all phenomena are empty, like illusions without reality, without any root."
(The Sutra of Holding the World,
Chapter Three on the Eighteen Natures)
The Buddha says:

"All phenomena are empty in essence, impermanent, and subject to destruction. Suppose a person in a night dream sees a lovely garden, mountains and rivers, crowds of people, dense forests and clear springs, halls and pavilions, all delightful; when he wakes
(wakes up)
, he sees nothing at all."
(The Sutra of the Kingly Dharma Spoken by the Buddha for King Prasenajit)
The Buddha says:
"Here no phenomenon arises, nor is there any phenomenon that ceases; without arising and without ceasing — this is the true nature of all phenomena."
(The Great Jewel Heap Sutra,
Volume Seventy-Seven)
The Buddha says:
"The great bodhisattvas contemplate all phenomena as without exception empty; this is to be awakened to and know the true nature of all phenomena."
(The Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra,
Volume Five Hundred Thirty-Seven)

blocks.text: 4. The True Nature of All Phenomena Is the One Dharma Seal

inline.s: The dharma seal is the seal of the Buddhadharma; it is the seal of truth handed down from Buddha to Buddha, the criterion of the Buddhadharma. Whatever does not accord with the dharma seal is not the Buddhadharma. The lesser vehicle is sealed by the "three dharma seals." The three dharma seals are: the seal of the impermanence of all conditioned things, the seal of the non-self of all phenomena, and the seal of the quiescence of nirvāṇa. The impermanence of all conditioned things means that all things in the world are at every moment in the process of arising, dwelling, changing, and ceasing; what existed in the past has now changed, and what exists now will in the end be illusory and destroyed. The non-self of all phenomena means that all phenomena have no substantial reality. The quiescence of nirvāṇa means that the state of nirvāṇa extinguishes all the suffering of birth and death and is unconditioned peace and bliss; hence nirvāṇa is quiescent.

The great vehicle is sealed by the "seal of true reality," which is also called the seal of the true nature of all phenomena. Since the true nature of all phenomena already encompasses the impermanence of all conditioned things, the non-self of all phenomena, and the quiescence of nirvāṇa, it is called the one dharma seal or the one seal of true reality. The great vehicle takes the exposition of the principle of the true nature of all phenomena as its foundation; to speak the Dharma apart from the true nature of all phenomena is all Mara's teaching. In the Lotus Sutra, the Buddha says:
"I adorn my body with the marks, my light illumines the world; revered by countless multitudes, I proclaim the seal of true reality."
The Buddhist Numerical Dictionary says:

"For the great Mahayana sutras spoken by the Tathagata all seal their teachings with the principle of true reality. Outsiders cannot adulterate them, heavenly maras cannot destroy them. If there is the seal of true reality, then it is the Buddha's teaching; if there is no seal of true reality, then it is Mara's teaching."
Master Zhiyi's Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra says:

"As for the lesser-vehicle sutras, if they bear the seal of the three seals of impermanence, non-self, and nirvāṇa, then they are the Buddha's teaching, and one who cultivates them attains the Way; if they lack the three dharma seals, then they are Mara's teaching. A Mahayana sutra has only one dharma seal, namely the true nature of all phenomena; it is called a sutra of definitive meaning and can lead one to the great Way. If it lacks the seal of true reality, it is Mara's teaching."
In his Textual Commentary on the Lotus Sutra he further says:

"The Buddhas awaken to the mark of true suchness and, riding this way of truth, appear in the world in response. They cause living beings to attain this true reality; it is solely for this matter that they appear in the world in response, and never for any other matter. Apart from the true nature of all phenomena, everything is called a matter of Mara."

In the sutras and treatises the phrase "neither arising nor ceasing" is often seen, yet it has two utterly different meanings. First, what outsiders mean by "neither arising nor ceasing" is: it has existed from the very beginning and is eternally indestructible. Second, what the Buddhadharma means by "neither arising nor ceasing" is: all things are illusory, and have never existed at all ("originally there is not a single thing"); since nothing has arisen, nothing ceases. The Buddha says:
"Here no phenomenon arises, nor is there any phenomenon that ceases; without arising and without ceasing — this is the true nature of all phenomena."
(The Great Jewel Heap Sutra, Volume Seventy-Seven)
In the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, the Sixth Patriarch gave a penetrating instruction on the Buddhadharma's meaning of neither arising nor ceasing:
"Jian said: You say neither arising nor ceasing — how does this differ from the outsiders? The Master
(the Sixth Patriarch)

said: What the outsiders call neither arising nor ceasing is to use ceasing to stop arising and to use arising to reveal ceasing; then ceasing is still not ceasing, and arising is said to be non-arising. What I call neither arising nor ceasing is that originally there is no arising, and now there is likewise no ceasing; therefore it is different from the outsiders."

(Translation: Xue Jian said: Master, you say neither arising nor ceasing — how does this differ from the outsiders? The Sixth Patriarch said: What the outsiders call neither arising nor ceasing is to use ceasing to put an end to arising and to use arising to manifest ceasing; in that case ceasing is like not ceasing, and arising is, so to speak, still non-arising. But what I call neither arising nor ceasing is that it was never there from the first ("originally there is not a single thing"), and therefore there is also no ceasing; hence it differs from the outsiders.)

What the Buddhadharma means by neither arising nor ceasing is this: all phenomena have never existed (they never arose, and therefore also do not cease) — and this is the true nature of all phenomena (the actual state of affairs of all phenomena). The Sutra of the Treasury of the Buddha,
Chapter Two on Buddha-Recitation, says:
"What is called the true nature of all phenomena? It is that all phenomena are ultimately empty, without anything whatsoever."
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
"All living beings, within the unborn, falsely see arising and ceasing; therefore it is called revolving in birth and death."
The Sutra of the Supreme King says:
"The unborn is real, the born is delusive. The foolish, drifting and drowning in birth and death; the Tathagata, realizing the real, is without delusion, and this is called nirvāṇa."
The Sutra of the Humane King says:
"All phenomena, in nature truly empty, neither come nor go, neither arise nor cease; they are identical with the ultimate reality and equal to the nature of phenomena."
In the Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra,
Volume Two Hundred Ninety-Six, the Buddha says:
"Subhuti
(Subhuti)

, in such a great treasure store of prajñāpāramitā, not the slightest phenomenon is spoken of as arising or ceasing, as defiled or pure, as grasped or abandoned. Why is this? Because not the slightest phenomenon can arise or cease, can be defiled or purified, can be grasped or abandoned."
The Heart Sutra says:
"All phenomena are empty in mark, neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing."

Therefore, what the Buddhadharma means by neither arising nor ceasing is the true nature of all phenomena; originally there is not a single thing, so how could there be any arising or ceasing to speak of? The Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra,
Chapter Eleven on the Study of Illusion, says:

"The Buddha told Subhuti: What do you think? Does an illusion have defilement or purity? No, World-Honored One. Subhuti! What do you think? Does an illusion have arising or ceasing? No, World-Honored One."
Question: Why is it said that "all phenomena are illusions"?

Answer: Because all living beings are within the dream of ignorance, and all phenomena are matters within the dream of ignorance. All the myriad things of the universe are hallucinations produced when a single deluded movement of thought loses the original nature. Yongjia's Song of Realizing the Way says:
"Within the dream, the six realms are clearly there; after awakening, all is empty and the great chiliocosm is gone."
(Within the dream of ignorance the six realms of rebirth are clearly there; when the dream of ignorance is awakened, all is limpid and quiescent, and the great chiliocosm simply does not exist.)
The Sutra of the Secret Adornment of the Great Vehicle says:
"Like forms in a dream
(sensory forms — referring to visible things)
, seen only through delusive thought; once awake, they do not exist
(nonexistent once the dream is over)
Within the dream of ignorance
one sees the various forms of men and women and so on; upon attaining perfect enlightenment
(attaining Buddhahood)
one sees nothing at all."

[Perfect enlightenment] True awakening; attaining Buddhahood is called attaining perfect enlightenment. [Upon attaining perfect enlightenment one sees nothing at all] Living beings, amid the limpid and unborn, see only arising and ceasing; the Buddhas, amid what is clearly arising and ceasing, see only the unborn.
In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the World-Honored One instructs that living beings are within the dream of ignorance:

"What is ignorance? Good sons! All living beings, from beginningless time, have had all kinds of inversions, like a confused person who mistakes the four directions for one another, falsely taking the four great elements as the mark of their own body and the shadowy traces of the six dusts as the mark of their own mind. It is like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good sons! The sky is truly without flowers; the diseased one falsely grasps them, and because of this false grasping he is not only deluded about the self-nature of this emptiness, but also deluded about where the real flowers arise. From this false existence he revolves in birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance. Good sons! This ignorance is not a real entity,
like a person in a dream

; while dreaming he is not nonexistent, but when he awakens he attains nothing at all. Like the flowers in the sky, which cease within the sky, one cannot say they have a fixed place of ceasing. Why? Because there is no place of arising. All living beings, within the unborn, falsely see arising and ceasing; therefore it is called revolving in birth and death."

[Four great elements] The great element of earth, the great element of water, the great element of fire, and the great element of wind. Earth has solidity as its nature, water has moisture as its nature, fire has warmth as its nature, and wind has movement as its nature. All tangible matter in the world has these four natures of solidity, moisture, warmth, and movement, and so they are called "great." The four great elements here refer to the body. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

"Constantly contemplate this: my present body is a convergence of the four great elements. Hair, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, brain, and filth all belong to earth; spittle, tears, pus, blood, fluids, phlegm, mucus, tears, semen, and excrement and urine all belong to water; warmth belongs to fire; movement belongs to wind. When the four great elements each separate, where will this false body be?"

[Shadowy traces of the six dusts] The various thoughts produced when the six sense faculties come into contact with the six dusts; since these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadowy traces of the six dusts — the phantom traces of the six dusts.
The Sutra of Divining the Good and Evil Karmic Retributions says:

"If among such living beings there are those who, through the perfuming of the dharma body and its power, have thinner afflictions, can grow weary of the world, seek the path of nirvāṇa, believe in and return to the one reality, and cultivate the six perfections and all the other factors of enlightenment, they are called bodhisattvas. If among such bodhisattvas there are those who fulfill the practice of all wholesome dharmas and are
ultimately able to leave the sleep of ignorance, they are then called Buddhas
It also says:
"Because all the practices of merit are fulfilled, one becomes a Buddha. That is to say, relying on the ultimate bodhisattva ground, one can remove all obstructions,
because the dream of ignorance
is exhausted."
The Sutra of the Kingly Dharma Spoken by the Buddha for King Prasenajit says:
"All phenomena are empty in essence, impermanent, and subject to destruction. Suppose a person,
in a night dream
, sees a lovely garden, mountains and rivers, crowds of people, dense forests and clear springs, halls and pavilions, all delightful; when he wakes
(wakes up)
he sees nothing at all."
Master Hanshan says:

"The self-nature of living beings is equal to that of the Buddha; originally it is undefiled, and it has no mark of birth and death, coming or going. But because of the first non-awakening, they are deluded about their original self-nature, and so it is called ignorance. Because of ignorance, all kinds of delusive thoughts arise, all kinds of inversions, creating all kinds of karma, and falsely grasping the suffering of birth and death in the three realms. All this is ignorance: not understanding one's own mind, one follows delusive thoughts and turns. It is like a person sound asleep having all kinds of nightmares, all kinds of states, all kinds of terror, unbearable in their many sufferings. And when he wakes, he seeks the matters of the dream and can find them nowhere. Therefore living beings fall into the
dream of ignorance
, follow delusive thoughts and inversions, create all kinds of karma, and bring all kinds of suffering upon themselves. Seen with awakened eyes, how could any of these inverted states be found?"
(From the Collection of Dream Wanderings,
Instruction to Dong Zhiguang)

[Three realms] The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the realm of formlessness. The realm of desire is the world inhabited by living beings who have the two desires of sexuality and food, and it includes, from the highest, the six heavens of desire, and in the middle, humans and animals, down to hungry ghosts and hells. The realm of form is the world inhabited by living beings who are free of the two desires of sexuality and food but still have a physical body, and it includes the four dhyanas and the eighteen heavens. The realm of formlessness is the world inhabited by living beings who no longer have a physical body but abide with their mind-consciousness in profound and subtle concentration, and it includes the four formless heavens (the heaven of infinite space, the heaven of infinite consciousness, the heaven of nothing whatsoever, and the heaven of neither perception nor non-perception). These three realms are all the domain of ordinary people's birth-and-death rebirth; therefore the first aim of Buddhist practitioners is to leave the three realms.
Master Hanshan says:
"The Buddha says:
all phenomena are like a dream, an illusion
. He also says: birth and death, nirvāṇa,
are like last night's dream
(From the Collection of Dream Wanderings,
Reply to Magistrate Yuan Cangru)
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:

"When this bodhisattva and living beings of the final age cultivate this mind and attain accomplishment, in this there is neither cultivation nor accomplishment. Perfect enlightenment shines universally, quiescent and non-dual
(the true nature of all phenomena)
; within it, the buddha worlds of hundreds of thousands of millions of asamkhyeyas, inexpressible in number, as many as the sands of the Ganges, are like flowers in the sky
(illusions)
, arising and ceasing in confusion. Neither identified with
(not dwelling in any phenomenon)
nor separate from
(not abandoning any phenomenon)
them, without bondage and without liberation; only then does one know that living beings are originally Buddhas, and that birth and death, nirvāṇa,
are like last night's dream

[Quiescent and non-dual] There is nothing whatsoever, and so it is called quiescent and non-dual. [Within it] Within the true realm of perfect enlightenment that is quiescent and non-dual. [Asamkhyeya] Translated into Chinese as "incalculable," it means so many that no number can calculate them. [Birth and death, nirvāṇa, are like last night's dream] Birth and death, nirvāṇa are all matters within the dream of ignorance; now that the dream of ignorance is awakened, looking back on past events is like last night's dream.
The Great Perfection of Wisdom Sutra,
Volume Five Hundred Seventy-Six, says:
"If all sentient beings could truly and thoroughly understand
that all phenomena are like illusions

, they should originally have already realized supreme enlightenment; but because sentient beings cannot comprehend that all phenomena are like illusions, they revolve in birth and death within the various destinies."
The Sutra of the Inconceivable State of the Tathagata of the Great Expanse says:
"All Tathagatas, relying on this samādhi, accomplish immeasurable great majestic power, and even realize and enter the emptiness of all phenomena
(all phenomena are illusions)

, and can manifest all kinds of sovereign deeds in all buddha lands of the ten directions. For example, suppose a person dreams of all kinds of transformations, and when he awakens, all that he saw is gone. Ordinary people are likewise: because of the
dream of ignorance

, they falsely give rise to the notion of substantial reality regarding all phenomena. The Buddhas, being awakened, are attached to nothing, and therefore can, in all worlds of the ten directions, in a single thought manifest immeasurable buddha deeds, sovereign and unobstructed, benefiting and bringing all living beings to accomplishment, causing them all to awaken and enter the immeasurable, profound, and wonderful gates of liberation."

All the sutras and treatises above are saying: living beings are deluded within the dream of ignorance, inverting and revolving; whereas the Buddhas have exhausted the dream of ignorance, are sovereign in regard to phenomena, and throughout the worlds of the ten directions manifest all kinds of buddha deeds to liberate living beings.
Master Hanshan's Collection of Dream Wanderings,
Reply to Magistrate Yuan Cangru, also says:
"Through the cultivation of bodhisattvas, even up to the seventh ground, they have not yet broken
the dream of ignorance

. Their teaching of living beings throughout and their accomplishment of pure lands are all buddha deeds within a dream. Therefore bodhisattvas of the eighth ground are like one crossing a river in a dream, still not abiding in awakening; only upon reaching Buddhahood is one called greatly awakened. This is stated clearly and fully recorded in the Avatamsaka Sutra, a plain and evident proof."

The dream of ignorance is a great dream, like a virtual world in which countless dreamers exist and can interact with one another, and can build and destroy their surroundings and the objects in them. Yet people find it hard to believe that they are in the dream of ignorance and that everything is an illusion. This is not strange: if you have never awakened, how could you know you are dreaming? Nevertheless, through the ages countless men who have clearly seen the mind and realized their nature have all confirmed that we are in the dream of ignorance. Master Yongjia's Song of Realizing the Way (Zhengdao Ge) says:
“In the dream the six realms plainly show; once wakened, all the vast world is empty and hollow.”
By practicing ourselves, we too can confirm this, and that is the repeatability of science.

[Reference] There is at present a view in the scientific community that the universe is a virtual world with an extremely intricate program. That program follows two basic principles (the rules of the game):

1. The principle of mental guidance. The moment the heart of the player moves, the system of this virtual world activates for him; when the player's heart remains still and unmoved, without even the subtlest thought, the system of this virtual world closes for him of itself. This is what is meant by all dharmas being mind-only: when the mind arises, various dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, various dharmas cease.

2. The principle of dynamic revision. In accord with what the player's avatar does in the virtual world, the system constantly revises and corrects his fate data, and by this determines his present condition and his future. If he has done good, his fate turns toward the good; if he has done evil, his fate turns toward the evil. Fate is always what one makes for oneself and receives of oneself — this is karmic retribution.
A dream, if you take it as real, will enslave you. Master Taixu said:
The mind within the dream
, that is the mind of the ordinary man;
the mind that knows it is dreaming within the dream
, that is the mind of the bodhisattva;
the mind that awakens
(waking from the dream)
that is the mind of the Buddha.”
(from the Outline of the Vijñaptimātratā View)
The Compendium of Mahāyāna Meanings (Dasheng Yizhang) says:

“Buddha is named for his virtue. Buddha means awareness and knowing, and from this the title is established. Awareness has two meanings. The first is called awareness-as-detection, as when a man detects a thief. The second is called awareness-as-awakening, as when a man wakes from sleep
(waking from sleep)

. Awareness-of-detection is set against the affliction obstacle; the harm wrought by afflictions is like a thief's, and only the sage's awareness knows not to be harmed by them, hence it is called awareness. The Nirvāṇa Sutra says: ‘As a man detects a thief and the thief can do nothing, so also is the Buddha.’ The awareness of awakening is set against the cognitive obstacle; the dark drowse of ignorance is like sleep, and when the sage's wisdom rises and there is suddenly great enlightenment,
as one wakes from sleep
(waking from a dream)

, hence it is called awareness. Being able to awaken oneself and also to awaken others, with awakening practice brought to its utmost fulfillment, is why it is called Buddha. To say he awakens himself sets him apart from ordinary men; to say he awakens others distinguishes him from the Two Vehicles; awakening practice brought to full consummation shows his difference from the bodhisattvas.”

[Affliction obstacle] Because ordinary people do not know the emptiness of self and cling to a self, and from that self spring greed, anger, delusion, and other afflictions, they thereby obstruct the manifestation of nirvāṇa; hence it is called an obstacle. [Knowledge obstacle] This is the cognitive obstacle. Because ordinary people do not know the emptiness of dharmas and cling to the various dharmas, they produce all sorts of erroneous knowledge that obstructs the arising of bodhi; hence it is called an obstacle. The sutra says: ‘If the attachment to dharmas is not removed, the cognitive obstacle arises and blocks bodhi.’
Therefore the practice should be pursued on two fronts: first, detection — to know the thought the instant it arises; second, awakening — no longer clinging to appearances.
Q: The Chan masters speak of ‘a dream within a dream.’ What does this mean?

Answer: The dream of ignorance is the first occurrence of the word ‘dream.’ The self-nature is the dreamer within the dream of ignorance, and because the self-nature deludedly clings to the physical body as itself and takes the shadows of the six sense-objects for its own mind, there therefore arise birth and death (birth-and-death in segments) and the cycle of rebirth — this is the second occurrence of the word ‘dream,’ the carrying on of the dream of rebirth within the dream of ignorance, which the ancients called ‘a dream within a dream.’ The five aggregates, body, and mind are the dreamers of the dream of rebirth. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
‘All beings, from beginnings beginning, are in all manner of upside-down confusion, like a lost man who takes the four directions to be in different places
(for example, taking east for west and south for north)

, and deludedly revere the four great elements as the form of a self and the shadows of the six sense-objects as the form of the self-mind. It is like one with diseased eyes who sees flowers in empty space
(flowers)
and a second moon. … From this false construction they turn about in birth and death.’
(For details see
A Detailed Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment

[Five aggregates] The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of volition, and the aggregate of consciousness — these five arise by accumulation, and so are called the ‘five aggregates’; and because they can cover over man's true nature, confusing and overturning him and driving him to create all manner of karma, they are also called the ‘five shrouds’ (five yin). Of these, the aggregate of form refers to matter, and is called ‘dharmas of form’; the four aggregates of feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness belong to the mental, and are called ‘dharmas of mind.’ These are the five great constituents of body and mind, of which the aggregate of form is the physical body while the other four (feeling, perception, volition, consciousness) are mind. [Four great elements] Earth, water, fire, and wind. Earth is hard in nature, water moist, fire warm, and wind moving. All the tangible things of the world possess these four natures — hardness, moisture, warmth, and motion — and so are called ‘great.’ [Shadows of the six sense-objects] The various imaginings produced when the six faculties meet the six sense-objects; because these imaginings are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadows of the six sense-objects — the phantom images of the six sense-objects.

When afflictions are completely cut off, one ends the birth-and-death of segments and leaves the dream of rebirth; when ignorance is completely cut off, one ends the birth-and-death of transformation and leaves the dream of ignorance.

[Birth-and-death in segments] Beings within the three realms and six destinies, owing to the good and evil karma they have created, have lifespans with fixed limits and bodies with fixed forms, and so their birth and death is called ‘birth-and-death in segments.’ One who ends birth-and-death in segments escapes the cycle and leaves the three realms. [Birth-and-death of transformation] The sages of the Three Vehicles have already cut off the delusions of view and thought and ended birth-and-death in segments. In the course of their practice, deluded imaginings gradually vanish while realization gradually grows; this passage from delusion to awakening differs in every stage, and the moving from an earlier stage into a later one is precisely like a birth-and-death, whose transformations are subtle and unfathomable beyond all thought — hence it is called ‘birth-and-death of transformation.’ One who ends birth-and-death of transformation perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.
Q: How does one leave the dream of rebirth?
Answer:

To leave this dream of rebirth, this endless round of birth and death, one must achieve it through practice. The common path is to cut off afflictions completely, so that at the moment of death one can be the master; then one can end birth and death and leave the cycle. The patriarch Huangbo says:
‘When a person is about to die, he should only contemplate that the five aggregates
(form, feeling, perception, volition, consciousness)

are all empty, that the four great elements have no self, that the true mind has no form and comes not nor goes. At birth the nature comes not; at death the nature goes not. Serenely one passes into serene nirvāṇa, mind and realm as one. If one can but understand this at once and at that very place, and be no longer bound by the three times, then one is a person who has left the world.’
(from the Essentials of the Transmission of Mind) If one cultivates the Pure Land path, one needs only sustain ten recitations at death (see details in
The Conditions for Rebirth
), and touch the response of Amitābha Buddha's coming to receive and guide one, then one leaves the dream of rebirth and is reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Q: It is said above that ‘all dharmas are illusions.’ Does that mean the ālaya-vijñāna is also an illusion?
Answer: Yes, the ālaya-vijñāna is an illusion. Because this question has long been a matter of considerable dispute, let me add a few citations here:
In the Vimalakīrti Sutra (Shuo Wugoucheng Jing), volume six, it speaks of ‘non-ālaya,’ and the Buddha says:
‘Though he delights in contemplating
non-ālaya
, he does not cast away the treasury of pure dharmas; though he contemplates that all dharmas are ultimately unborn, he still bears the burden of benefiting sentient beings.’
In the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra, volume 576, it also speaks of ‘non-ālaya,’ and Mañjuśrī (the bodhisattva of wondrous auspiciousness) says:

‘All sentient beings may be established in the Buddha's wondrous Dharma, in the awakening of wisdom that is unmoved, knowing the nature of dharmas to be empty — without name and without form, without support and without abiding, without grasping and without attachment, without obstruction and without clinging, like empty space,
non-ālaya

, and non-niyanta; the supreme still, the utmost still; unborn and unceasing, undefiled and immaculate, uncompleted and undestroyed, neither existing nor non-existent. Thereby one attains in it the profound patience (kṣānti) and is never far from the Buddha's wondrous Dharma.’
[Niyanta] A different name for greed, meaning the utmost insatiable craving that knows no end.
The scriptural passages above all state that the ālaya-vijñāna is not real, but is an illusion.

In his Treatise on the Hundred Dharmas of the Mahāyāna, Bodhisattva Vasubandhu groups all dharmas into five great categories: dharmas of mind, dharmas of mind-mental factors, dharmas not associated with mind, and unconditioned dharmas. The ālaya-vijñāna belongs to the category of mind-dharmas among all dharmas. The Buddha says:
‘All dharmas are like an illusion, like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a flame.’
(from the Small Perfection of Wisdom Sutra, volume ten) And the Buddha says:
‘Know that all dharmas are empty, like an illusion without reality, having no root.’

(from the Sutra of the Keeper of the World, the eighteenth, chapter on the nature of dharmas, third.) Since all dharmas are like an illusion without reality, and the ālaya-vijñāna is one dharma among all dharmas, it is of course like an illusion without reality.
Q: Why, in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra, does the Buddha say:
‘The true self that the Tathāgata speaks of today is called the Buddha-nature.’
Answer: The ‘true self’ spoken of here is relative to the false self of the five aggregates, body, and mind. In the Tenth Chapter on the Bequeathed Teaching, the Sixth Patriarch says:
‘Only recognize your own original mind and see your own original nature, unmoving and still, unborn and unceasing.’
And the meaning of ‘unborn and unceasing’ is that originally there were none, exactly as the Sixth Patriarch explains ‘unborn and unceasing’ in the Ninth Chapter on the Dharma of Protection:
‘Originally there was no birth, and now there is no ceasing.’
In the Sutra of the Buddha's Treasury, the Buddha says:
‘All dharmas are unborn and unceasing, without form, without activity.’
This shows that the original nature (namely, the tathāgatagarbha, the Buddha-nature) is also an illusion.
Q: If this is so, is the dharmakāya itself also an illusion?
Answer: The Mahāyāna Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground (Xin Di Guan Jing) says:
‘Always contemplate the Buddha's wondrous dharmakāya, whose essence and nature are like empty space, ungraspable.’
The Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sutra says:
‘The dharmakāya is like an illusion or a dream — how can it be praised? Knowing the nature to be without self-nature and unborn, that is what is called praising the Buddha.’
Q: Then who is bound? Who creates karma? Who transmigrates? Who is liberated? And to where is one liberated?

Answer: The self-nature is bound; the self-nature creates karma; the self-nature transmigrates; the self-nature is liberated. Liberation has two stages: if one ends birth-and-death in segments, one leaves the cycle and escapes the three realms; if one ends birth-and-death of transformation, one perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. As for where one is liberated, according to the levels of liberation there are four lands where one may dwell: the land where ordinary men and sages dwell together, the land of expedient remainder, the land of real reward and adornment, and the land of eternal stillness and light. The land where ordinary men and sages dwell together is the land inhabited by ordinary men together with sages who manifest bodies and preach the Dharma for the sake of teaching sentient beings; the land of expedient remainder is the land of the Two Vehicles and of bodhisattvas who have not yet realized the dharmakāya; the land of real reward and adornment is the land of the Buddha's reward-body and of the bodhisattvas on the grounds; the land of eternal stillness and light is the land where the Buddha's pure dharmakāya manifests quiescence. All four lands are doings within the dream of ignorance. A self-nature of a higher level may go to a lower land, but a self-nature of a lower level cannot go to a higher land. After attaining Buddhahood, one may either remain in the dream of ignorance to teach and save sentient beings, or enter extinction, whereupon that dreamer no longer dreams the dream of ignorance. (For a fuller account of the self-nature, see
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha
Q: The saying ‘Neither mind, nor Buddha, nor things’ — what does it mean?
Answer:
The Compendium of the Five Lamps records:
A monk asked, ‘Why does the Master say
mind is Buddha
?’ The Master
(Mazu)
said, ‘To stop the infant's crying
(this is an expedient saying for those just beginning to study)
.’ The monk said, ‘When the crying stops, how then?’ The Master said, ‘
not mind, not Buddha
.’ The monk said, ‘Apart from these two kinds of people, how do you instruct them?’ The Master said, ‘Say to him
(him)
say
not a thing

[ To stop the infant's crying ] This is a metaphor for the expedient teaching (not the final teaching). When a child cries, an adult gives him a yellow poplar leaf, saying, ‘This is a gold piece; you may take it to buy sweets.’ The child holds it and stops crying. The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra,
Volume Twenty,
says:

‘As when an infant cries, the parents give it a yellow poplar leaf and say: “Don't cry! Don't cry! I shall give you gold.” The infant, seeing it, thinks it is real gold and stops crying; yet this poplar leaf is not really gold.’
The Compendium of the Five Lamps further records:
The Chan master Zizai of Funiu Mountain at Yique, of the Li family of Wuxing, first followed the master Guoyi, and after receiving full ordination studied under Mazu and awakened to the mind-ground
(enlightenment)
. Mazu had him deliver a letter to the National Master Zhong
(National Master Huizhong)
. The National Master asked, ‘What Dharma does the great master Ma use to show his disciples?’ The master said, ‘
mind is Buddha
.’ The National Master said, ‘What kind of talk is that
(he greatly disapproved)
!’ After a long while
(a long time passed)
he asked again, ‘Besides this, is there any further teaching?’ The master said, ‘
not mind, not Buddha
. Or it is said:
neither mind, nor Buddha, nor a thing.
’ The National Master said, ‘That is a little closer
(that is about right)
In the kōan above three stages are set forth:
‘mind is Buddha’
‘not mind, not Buddha’
‘neither mind, nor Buddha, nor a thing’

. The ‘mind’ spoken of here refers to the self-nature. ‘Mind is Buddha’ means that the Buddha is nothing other than this: the self-nature that is fully awakened is the Buddha. ‘Not mind, not Buddha’ means that the self-nature and the Buddha are both illusions, doings within the dream of ignorance. ‘Neither mind, nor Buddha, nor a thing’ speaks of the one who dreams the dream of ignorance.
Q:
All sentient beings are originally Buddhas; since they are Buddhas, why do they give rise to ignorance and sink into being sentient beings?

Answer: All sentient beings originally possess the Tathāgata's wisdom and adorned nature, which is why they are said to be ‘originally Buddhas,’ yet there remains the fundamental ignorance in a latent state. Once it manifests (a single thought of non-awakening) and one enters the dream of ignorance, one sinks into being a sentient being. The process is: a single thought of non-awakening gives rise to the three subtle aspects, and the realm of objects serves as the condition for the growth of the six coarse aspects. (For details see
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha
Q: If ignorance is said to be originally present, then since ignorance exists, how can one be said to have attained Buddhahood?

Answer: Although the original Buddha has fundamental ignorance, that fundamental ignorance is in a latent state, and so he still possesses the Tathāgata's wisdom and adorned nature. Since he possesses the Tathāgata's wisdom and adorned nature, he is of course a Buddha.

Q: All sentient beings were originally already Buddhas, and later gave rise to ignorance, entered the dream of ignorance, and sank into being sentient beings. Now we are practicing — after we attain Buddhahood, at what time shall we again give rise to ignorance, enter the dream of ignorance, and sink into being sentient beings?

Answer: When we now practice to attain Buddhahood, the aim is to eradicate fundamental ignorance. So one who eradicates fundamental ignorance and attains Buddhahood will never again give rise to ignorance, enter the dream of ignorance, or sink into being a sentient being. This is like a man who, before he has had smallpox, is a healthy person; having had smallpox he falls into being a patient, and after he recovers he is again a healthy person and, indeed, with lifelong immunity, so he will never again contract smallpox. Concerning this, in the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment the Buddha teaches:

‘Good man! As when ore is smelted with gold, the gold does not come into being because of the smelting; once it has become gold, it does not again turn to ore. … The Tathāgata's perfect enlightenment is likewise.’
(Translation: Good man! As when gold ore is smelted, the gold does not come into being because of the smelting; once it is smelted into pure gold, it will not again become ore.
The Tathāgata's perfect enlightenment is also thus (it does not reverse).)

[Fundamental ignorance] From the beginningless beginning a single thought of non-awakening causes one to enter the dream of ignorance, to be dazed through the long night, unable to understand the truth, and to give rise to all delusions and afflictions. This is fundamental ignorance, also called beginningless ignorance. The Mahāyāna Scripture of the Meaning of the Six Perfections says:

‘As the fierce flame of fire borne on the wind can be restrained, and the waves of the ocean can likewise be stilled, only the deluded mind is very hard to subdue. Why? Because from beginningless ignorance it is deluded about the nature of the mind.’
Q: ‘When the mind arises, various dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, various dharmas cease’ — what does this mean?
Answer:

‘When the mind arises, various dharmas arise’ means that the mind arises and one enters the dream of ignorance; ‘when the mind ceases, various dharmas cease’ means that the mind ceases and the dream of ignorance is awakened from. The Song of Realizing the Way says:
‘In the dream the six realms plainly show; once wakened, all the vast world is empty and hollow.’
The Mahāyāna Ghanavyūha Sutra says:
‘As the forms in a dream
(form-objects — the visible things)
are only deluded viewings of thought, on waking
(awakening from sleep)
they are without existence; [so too] while the dream of ignorance
and seeing the various forms of men and women and the like, upon perfect enlightenment there is nothing to be seen.’
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
‘This ignorance does not have a real substance, like a man in a dream — while dreaming it is not without, and upon waking nothing is obtained.’
The Sutra in Which the Buddha Speaks the Dharma of Kings to King Suvarṇaprabhāsa says:

‘All dharmas are empty in essence and nature, impermanent, decaying and destroyed. It is like a person who in a night dream sees fine gardens, mountains, rivers, crowds, dense forests, clear springs, halls, houses, towers, and pavilions, all delightful, and when he wakes
(awakening from sleep)
he sees nothing at all.’
The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna says:
Therefore the three realms are false and illusory, made by mind alone; apart from mind there are no six sense-object realms. What is the meaning of this? Because all dharmas arise from
mind giving rise to false thoughts

. All discrimination is the discrimination of one's own mind; mind does not see mind, and there is nothing to be apprehended. Know that all the realms of the world exist dependent upon the ignorant deluded mind of sentient beings. Therefore all dharmas, like images in a mirror, have no substance to be apprehended; they are only the mind's falseness,
because when the mind arises various dharmas arise, and when the mind ceases various dharmas cease

Translation: Therefore the three realms are an illusion (false and unreal), made only by the mind's imagining (entering the dream of ignorance, the six sense-object realms appear); apart from the mind there are no six sense-object realms (the dream of ignorance being awakened from, there are no six sense-object realms). What does this mean? Because all dharmas arise from the mind giving rise to false thoughts. All discrimination is merely the discrimination of one's own mind; mind does not see mind, and there is nothing to be apprehended. Know that all the realms of the world exist dependent upon the ignorant deluded mind (the dreaming mind) of sentient beings. Therefore all dharmas, like images in a mirror, have no substance to be apprehended; it is only the mind dreaming the dream of ignorance, because when the mind arises (entering the dream of ignorance) various dharmas arise (various realms appear), and when the mind ceases (the dream of ignorance awakened from) various dharmas cease (various realms cease).

[Therefore the three realms are false, made by mind alone; apart from mind there are no six sense-object realms] The three realms are doings within the dream of ignorance; once the dream is awakened from, there are no six sense-object realms.
Concerning
‘the three realms are false, made by mind alone’
and
‘when the mind arises various dharmas arise, when the mind ceases various dharmas cease’
, the Sutra of Divining Karmic Retribution (Zhan Cha Shan'e Yebao Jing) says:
‘Furthermore, know that the forms outside the mind
(the forms of the external realms within the mind)
like the various realms seen in a dream,
are made only by the mind's thought
(what the dreaming mind sees)
, with no real external events. All realms are likewise, for they all arise dependent upon seeing within
the dream of ignorance-consciousness
, being produced by false imagining
(this is what false imagining produces)
. Moreover, know that the inner mind is unceasing from thought to thought
(gross thought, subtle thought, or the subtlest thought, thought following thought without break)
, so that all realms seen and perceived likewise follow the mind in unceasing thought after thought
(continuing without break)
, according to the saying:
When the mind arises, various dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, various dharmas cease.’
[When the mind arises, various dharmas arise; when the mind ceases, various dharmas cease]

‘When the mind arises, various dharmas arise’ means that the mind arises (the initial stirring of thought) and one enters the dream of ignorance, so various dharmas appear; ‘when the mind ceases, various dharmas cease’ means that the mind ceases (the subtlest thought ceases) and the dream of ignorance is awakened from, so the various dharmas seen in the dream cease. Therefore ‘mind arises’ here refers to the initial stirring of thought, and ‘mind ceases’ refers to the cessation of the subtlest thought.
[Initial stirring of thought] This is

fundamental ignorance, also called beginningless ignorance. By this single stirring of thought one enters the dream of ignorance, dazed through the long night, unable to understand the truth, and so gives rise to delusion and creates karma, and thereby receives karmic retribution and turns about in birth and death. [Subtle thought] The subtle arising and ceasing of the consciousness-mind, which is the mark of the ālaya-vijñāna. The Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna says:
‘When the bodhisattva's stage is exhausted
(having completed the ten stages)

, and the expedient means are fulfilled, then in a single thought of responding the awakening mind first arises, and the mind has no first mark; because one is far from subtle thought, one sees the mind-nature, and the mind is then forever abiding — this is called ultimate awakening.’
Q: Since all dharmas are illusory, body and mind are also illusions, and practice is also an illusion, then why practice? And who practices?

Answer: Although we are in the dream of ignorance and all dharmas are illusory, your actual experience is nonetheless very real: birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, worry, calamities from heaven, disasters from men — none of these feels in the least illusory to you, just as when you are in a night dream and have not yet awakened. Therefore the purpose of practice is to awaken from the dream of ignorance (to attain Buddhahood), thoroughly to escape these sufferings of life after life, and to save and deliver all sentient beings who undergo such suffering. Practice is the self-nature's own practicing — it is using illusion to train away illusion, so that when illusion is exhausted the dream awakens. This principle the Buddha sets forth incisively in the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment; see, in
A Detailed Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment
, the chapter on the ‘illusion-like samādhi.’

Since one practices illusion with illusion, and the aim is that illusion be exhausted and the dream awaken, one must not practice apart from the phenomenal matters within the dream of ignorance, and yet one must not be deluded by the phenomenal matters and cling to them as real.

In practice there are frequently two deviations: first, leaning toward non-existence, denying the phenomenal matters and falling into annihilation; second, clinging to existence, deluded by phenomenal matters as real and being carried about by them. What is right is the Middle Way, which leans neither to non-existence nor to attachment: earnestly practice the six perfections and the myriad conducts while at the same time being free of appearances. Therefore in the sutras and treatises the teaching is often set forth simultaneously from the two viewpoints of the real mark of all dharmas and of the phenomenal matters of the dream of ignorance (the six sense-object realms). If one does not grasp this point, one is forever beset by doubt: why speak of non-existence at one moment and of existence at the next? Is it ultimately non-existence, or existence? In truth, ‘non-existence’ is spoken with regard to the essence and nature (the essential nature) — this is the real mark of all dharmas, what is called ‘serenely unborn, all dharmas one mark’; ‘existence’ is spoken with regard to the phenomenal matters of the dream of ignorance (the six sense-object realms), what is called ‘a many-splendored array of myriad phenomena, arising and ceasing in full array.’

[The Middle Way] Not leaning to non-existence, not leaning to existence; neither non-existence nor existence, yet also neither without non-existence nor without existence; not falling into either extreme; perfectly fused and unobstructed — this is called the Middle Way.

A thing has three aspects: essence, form, and function. The essence is the essential nature, also called the nature or the essence-nature; the essence of a thing is utterly empty, wholly without anything, and this is the common real mark of all dharmas, often described with words such as ‘true thusness is equal, unborn and unceasing, neither increasing nor decreasing, ultimately ever-present.’ ‘True thusness is equal’ means that the essence-nature (true thusness) of all dharmas is equal to one another, all alike being utterly empty and without anything; ‘unborn and unceasing, neither increasing nor decreasing, ultimately ever-present’ is a depiction of being utterly empty and without anything. The form is the appearance of the thing in the dream of ignorance, and the function is the working of the thing in the dream of ignorance.

[True thusness] Zhen (true) means real and genuine; ru (thusness) means abiding as always. The essence-nature of all dharmas, free of the false and real, is therefore called true; ever-abiding, unchanging and unaltered, it is therefore called thusness. [Unborn and unceasing, neither increasing nor decreasing, ultimately ever-present] ‘Unborn and unceasing’ — all dharmas are utterly empty, without anything; since they never existed at all, of course they are unborn and also unceasing. ‘Neither increasing nor decreasing’ — all dharmas are utterly empty, without anything, so of course there is no speaking of increase or decrease. ‘Ultimately ever-present’ — ‘ever-present’ describes there being no arising, ceasing, or change; all dharmas being utterly empty and without anything, they are naturally ultimately ever-present.

The Mahāyāna practitioner must both know the forms and functions and understand the essence-nature; must gather the forms back into the nature (gather the phenomenal matters back into the essence-nature), be free of appearances and without abiding, and not be turned by the realms.
As for the principle of being free of appearances and without abiding, the Buddha sets it forth very thoroughly in the Diamond Sutra, for example:
‘If a bodhisattva has the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a lifespan, he is not a bodhisattva.’
This says that a bodhisattva must be free of the four marks.
‘If a bodhisattva gives without dwelling in marks, his merit and virtue are immeasurable.’

This says that giving should be free of marks. Because of the six perfections (giving, precepts, patience, vigor, meditation, and prajñā), giving ranks first, and here giving represents the six perfections.
‘A bodhisattva should be free of all marks and give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.’
This says: on the path of bodhi, from the very beginning, at the very moment of giving rise to the mind, one must be free of marks.
When Subhuti put the question:
‘World-Honored One! If a good man or good woman gives rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, on what should they abide? How should they subdue their mind?’
The Buddha answered:

‘A good man or good woman who gives rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi should give rise to such a thought: I should bring all sentient beings to extinction, and having brought all sentient beings to extinction, there is yet not a single sentient being truly brought to extinction.’
So the answer to ‘On what should they abide? How should they subdue their mind?’ is: be free of appearances and without abiding, and so ferry sentient beings across.
‘One should not give rise to a mind abiding in forms, nor should one give rise to a mind abiding in sounds, scents, tastes, touch, or dharmas; one should give rise to the mind that abides nowhere.’
This says: do not give rise to mind by abiding in the sense-object realms, and when mind is given rise to, let it not abide in the sense-object realms.
‘By practicing all good dharmas with no self, no person, no sentient being, and no lifespan, one obtains anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.’
This says: being free of the four marks and practicing any good dharma, one realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.

(This passage says that the key to attaining anuttara-samyak-sambodhi is the absence of the four marks, and not the particular kind of good dharma one practices. The good dharma practiced without the four marks is the unconditioned dharma. The World-Honored One here reveals to us the universal principle of attaining anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, from which we may also know how crucial and how important it is to be free of the four marks!)
Apart from all marks, one is named a Buddha.”

Question: What is meant by “dependent origination, empty nature”?

Answer: “Dependent origination” means that all things in the world arise from the coming together of many conditions. “Empty nature” means that the dharmas produced by the coming together of many conditions are empty in their essence, having no truly existent self-entity of their own, like things in a dream.
Question: What are conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas?
Answer: Dharmas produced by causes and conditions are called “conditioned dharmas”; dharmas not produced by causes and conditions are called “unconditioned dharmas.”
Question: Many sutras and treatises speak of all dharmas as having no self-nature. Why, then, does the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra say,
“For instance, an ox has no nature of a horse, and a horse has no nature of an ox; yet it is not that they have no nature at all”

Answer: The term “self-nature” has three meanings. First, the essence of a thing (its substance), that is, the true reality of all dharmas. Second, the inner spiritual capacity of sentient beings (see
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha
). Third, the attribute of a thing.
[Attribute] The quality inherent in a thing itself; a necessary, basic, and inseparable characteristic of that thing.

Polysemy in language and writing satisfies the principle of economy in language — with a limited vocabulary it reflects the infinite variety of objective things — but it also creates a certain difficulty for our understanding. Therefore, when reading, one must judge from the context which meaning a polysemous word bears in that place.
The passage of sutra text you ask about comes from the Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sutra:

“Mahāmati! As I have taught that all dharmas are without self, it is because within all dharmas there is no nature of a self that I teach that they are without self; it is not that all dharmas have no self-nature of their own. The meaning of the Tathāgata's words should be understood in the same way. Mahāmati! For instance, an ox has no nature of a horse, and a horse has no nature of an ox; yet it is not that they have no nature at all.”

Its meaning is this: Mahāmati, when I teach that all dharmas are without self, it is because within all dharmas there is no essence of a self that I teach that all dharmas are without self (that is, all dharmas are illusions), and not that all dharmas have no attributes of their own. The meaning of the words spoken by the Buddhas and Tathāgatas should be understood in the same way. Mahāmati! For instance, an ox has no attribute of a horse, and a horse has no attribute of an ox; yet it is not that all dharmas have no attributes of their own.
In the passage of sutra text above, “self-nature” means the attribute of a thing.

In this passage, “all dharmas are without self” is spoken with regard to the true reality of all dharmas, meaning that all dharmas are illusions. But here, “all dharmas are not without self-nature (all dharmas are not without attributes of their own)” is spoken with regard to the attributes of the myriad forms in the dream of ignorance. The central idea of this passage is this: fundamentally speaking, all dharmas do not exist (“all dharmas are without self”); yet with regard to the world of forms in the dream of ignorance, they do have attributes of their own (“all dharmas are not without self-nature”). The former is spoken with regard to the essence of all dharmas, the latter with regard to the marks of all dharmas.

All dharmas are without self” is also often expressed in the sutras and treatises as “all dharmas have no self-nature (all dharmas have no essence of their own),” meaning that all dharmas have no substantial reality and are all illusions, like things in a dream. For example, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sutra says:

“For this reason, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, when practicing the prajñāpāramitā, grasps at any dharma as existent, or as nonexistent, or as both existent and nonexistent, or as neither nonexistent nor non-nonexistent, or does not grasp at all, he is not practicing the prajñāpāramitā. Why is this? Because
(that is, because)
all dharmas are utterly without self-nature and cannot be grasped.”
Here the meaning of self-nature is the essence of a thing
(its substance)
, that is, the true reality of all dharmas.
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“When the self-nature is deluded, one is an ordinary being; when the self-nature is awakened, one is a Buddha.”
Here the meaning of self-nature is the inner spiritual capacity of sentient beings.
